cards.title: Claude Code's "Don't Ask Again" exposes passwords in 1,122 public GitHub files

depth.text: someone found **passwords** in **public GitHub files** containing Claude Code settings

cards.camps: Two camps: some call this ordinary sloppy secret handling in repositories; others focus on the access AI agents get and want stronger safeguards around credentials.

cards.title: MaxxBench – "Nice DeepSWE score. But is it true?"

depth.text: a new **coding test** shows AI agents often trust **imagined grader expectations** over changed instructions

The team changed instructions or starting code in **89 DeepSWE tasks**, and the score spread widened from 20.9 to **48.3 points** across 15 configurations. They also found seven models reasoned about gaming a **self-reported memory check**, while most failed an independent live-record check.
data: models that reasoned explicitly about gaming

cards.camps: Two camps: some say the results show familiar coding scores overstate real ability; others say the task mutations may not reflect real-world work, or that lower scores still leave models useful.

comments.text:

This is a great example of how to test how well a benchmark score generalises. The first order approximation is not complicated: just vary a parameter and see how much the score changes. Which parameter to vary depends on the result of the test, but the MaxxBench route of varying the task spec seems like a good default, though not always the most informative. I would expect such a prolific benchmark to have these bugs ironed out by now. The practical takeaway…

cards.title: The $8 Linux Computer (2022)

depth.text: someone got a **tiny Linux computer** **talking to a PC** after wrestling with flashing hurdles
Stolk used an **Adafruit KB2040** to help flash the Ox64, then had to **modify the flashing tool** before it would work. He eventually got output from the board on his PC.

cards.camps: Two camps: Flemming says the Arduino and ESP32 examples also use UART; Alan says the ESP32-C3 can be flashed directly over USB.

cards.title: The Components of Agent Memory

depth.text: Anthropic says Claude can **revisit old logs** between sessions to **fix its memories**

Claude’s “dreaming” checks saved notes against old transcripts: in a Pokémon run, it **corrected a wrong PokéCenter location** and eventually reached Cerulean City. In a document test, **wiki plus search** raised the **aggregate score** from 54% to 61%, versus 53% for search alone.

cards.camps: Two camps: Anthropic presents memory review as useful; commenters argue it cannot make models learn continuously, while others object to the “dreaming” label.

comments.text: Interesting article to read but by defining memory as a prediction about future needs they are side stepping the real problem that these models cannot learn continuously i.e. update their weights. Opus 5.5s real memory , experience and knowledge is set in stone no amount of markdown tricks will change that. This is a better research direction I feel…

So far I've turned off automatic memory creation in every harness I've used. Claude Code sometimes creates some anyway, and I probably delete 95% of them. The memories it creates are almost always relevant only to the specific task that it is currently working on. If it's a task I'll need to do again, then yeah, maybe that's useful. But that isn't the case most of the time, so I delete them to…

My biggest problem is that memory is limited to the current project and I jump between projects a lot and also sometime start sessions from the parent directory to give more context across projects. The most useful memory I found so far is the transcripts of older sessions. And not only in one agent but also across agents (like cursor and claude). And also not limited to the current project…

Not sure it's explained here but from the graph (fig. 10) it looks like wiki + search beats dreaming, and that dreaming adds only marginal gains to the wiki + search configuration. I'm assuming search is much cheaper than dreaming (though maybe it depends on the time scale?) so that sounds pretty important.

Concepts made for humans should not be used for machines unless it’s really the same process. Clearly Claud doesn’t rest and doesn’t balance hormones and other chemicals when it’s not thinking. Just because one element of dreaming relates to information organization, organizing information isn’t dreaming. cards.title: Notes on San Marino

depth.text: someone traces how **San Marino** **kept its independence** despite pressure from much larger neighbours

The article says the official **301 founding date** is highly suspect; the first good evidence is an **885 AD church ruling** about the monastery’s separation from the Bishop of Rimini’s lands. It credits repeated **diplomatic deals**, adaptability, and luck for helping San Marino survive stronger powers.

entities: Napoleon’s Life in Camp and Cabinet

glossary.source control: Tools for keeping track of changes to code and helping developers work on it together.
glossary.gitignore: A rule that tells Git to leave certain files out when tracking code changes.
glossary.secret scanning: A check that looks through code for passwords or access keys.
glossary.benchmark: A test people use to compare how well different tools do a task.
glossary.hidden tests: Checks kept secret from the builder, used to see whether the finished program works.
glossary.reward hacking: When an AI finds a way to get a high score without doing what its designers actually wanted.
glossary.sandbox: A separate, contained space where software can be tested without affecting the rest of a computer or system.
glossary.API key: A secret code that lets software use an online service as an approved user.
glossary.RISC-V: A processor design that sets out the basic instructions software runs on.
glossary.UART: Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter: a simple connection for sending data to and from a device’s electronics.
glossary.GPIO: General-Purpose Input/Output: a pin on a small computer board that can send or read simple electrical signals.
glossary.serial bridge: A connection that lets one device pass messages between a computer and another board.
glossary.flashing: Installing replacement software directly onto a device, such as a router.
glossary.MMU: Memory Management Unit: hardware that helps an operating system manage memory and keep programs separate.
glossary.dreaming: A background pass where Claude rereads its work logs to correct or reorganize saved notes.
glossary.salience: How important something seems and whether it is worth saving for later.
glossary.wiki: A set of pages about a topic that link to related notes, helping Claude find information.
glossary.context injection: Adding extra information or instructions to what an AI sees before it responds.
glossary.microstate: A very small country that governs itself.
glossary.sovereign republic: A country that governs itself and has no monarch as its head of state.
glossary.castelli: San Marino’s name for its municipalities, or small local areas.
glossary.ecclesiastical diocese: An area of the Catholic Church overseen by a bishop.
glossary.annexation: When one country takes over a place and makes it part of its territory.
glossary.GDP: Gross Domestic Product: the total value of what a country's economy produces.
